title: Confinement and String Breaking in the Compact Abelian Higgs Model
summary: While real-time simulation of Quantum Chromodynamics remains technologically out of reach, simplified models for studying elements of QCD phenomenology abound. This work presents a simple model, a spin-1 truncation of the Compact Abelian Higgs Model simulated on qutrit sites, in which confinement and string breaking is accessible to current simulation methods. In the low-energy regime of 1+1D scalar electrodynamics, the heavy modes are integrated out, producing a spin chain effective Hamiltonian in which Gauss' law is implicitly satisfied. We study the spectrum of string-like excitations using DMRG methods on the order of 100 sites. We demonstrate that an added, local chemical potential, playing a role analogous to external charges, permits parameter-dependent measurements of physical features of interest like the string tension and effective meson mass. Varying the chemical potential also permits a characterization of string stability not assessed in prior studies of confining lattice models.

AI.tldr: A simplified model, a spin-1 truncation of the Compact Abelian Higgs Model, is presented and simulated to study confinement and string breaking in QCD. The model uses DMRG methods on qutrit sites and allows for the measurement of physical features such as string tension and effective meson mass through the adjustment of a local chemical potential.
AI.motivation: To provide a simplified, accessible model for studying Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) phenomena, particularly confinement and string breaking, which are not yet achievable with real-time QCD simulations due to technological limitations.
AI.method: The researchers use a spin-1 truncation of the Compact Abelian Higgs Model, simulate it on qutrit sites, and apply DMRG methods to a 100-site system. They incorporate a local chemical potential to measure and characterize the string stability and other physical properties like string tension and effective meson mass.
AI.result: The study successfully demonstrates that the addition of a local chemical potential enables the measurement of key physical features such as string tension and effective meson mass. It also shows that varying the chemical potential can be used to characterize string stability, which was not possible in previous studies of confining lattice models.
AI.conclusion: This work presents a novel approach to simulating and understanding elements of QCD phenomenology, specifically confinement and string breaking, using a simplified model that is within reach of current simulation technologies. The method provides a way to measure and characterize important physical features by adjusting a local chemical potential.

title: Pion Transition Form Factor in Lattice QCD
summary: We investigate the neutral pion transition form factor $F_{π^0γ^\astγ^\ast}(q_1^2,q_2^2)$ in lattice QCD and confirm that the connected and disconnected contributions have the same sign. We employ the recently proposed blending method, which supplies an unbiased and cheap estimators for the required all-to-all propagators. The external pion states are treated within the distillation framework, while the electromagnetic currents are evaluated in the full blending space. Numerical tests are performed on an $N_f=2+1$ lattice ensemble. Our result shows that the contribution of the disconnected part is approximately $1\%$ of that of the connected part and enables constructive interference of probability amplitudes.

AI.tldr: The study confirms the same sign for connected and disconnected contributions in the neutral pion transition form factor using lattice QCD, with the disconnected part contributing about 1% of the connected part, allowing for constructive interference.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to investigate the neutral pion transition form factor within lattice QCD and to determine the relative contributions and signs of the connected and disconnected parts, which is important for understanding the underlying dynamics of the process.
AI.method: The method involves the use of a recently proposed blending technique for an unbiased and efficient estimation of all-to-all propagators. The external pion states are handled with the distillation framework, and electromagnetic currents are computed in the full blending space, with numerical tests on an $N_f=2+1$ lattice ensemble.
AI.result: The results indicate that the disconnected contribution is around 1% of the connected contribution, and both have the same sign, leading to constructive interference of probability amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that the blending method successfully provides a viable approach for estimating the disconnected contributions, and the findings support the theoretical expectation of constructive interference between the connected and disconnected amplitudes.

title: On credit attribution and research software: A case study from lattice QCD
summary: Questions of authorship, credit attribution, and the recognition of research software contributions have become increasingly prominent in those constantly growing research areas for which software constitutes an essential part of the research process. While general guidelines and best practices exist, their application in concrete situations often raises nontrivial interpretative and procedural issues. This article presents a documented case study from lattice QCD research, illustrating how the development of numerical strategies, long-term software infrastructure, and conceptual extensions of existing work can give rise to complex questions of authorship, priority, and credit attribution. Rather than discussing the underlying scientific results, the focus is on the sequence of events, the role of software as a long-term research infrastructure, and the interaction with established mechanisms for credit attribution and research integrity assessment. The aim of this work is to contribute to transparency and discussion on how current practices and guidelines are applied in realistic collaborative environments, and to highlight structural tensions that may arise between open scientific collaboration, software sustainability, and traditional notions of authorship. The article is intended as a factual account and reflection on research practice, and aims to stimulate discussion on whether additional community standards for recognising long-term research software contributions may be beneficial within lattice QCD.

AI.tldr: This article examines a case study from lattice QCD research, focusing on the complexities of authorship, priority, and credit attribution in relation to the development of research software. It aims to foster transparency and discussion about current practices and their application in real-world collaborative settings, while also considering the balance between open collaboration, software sustainability, and traditional authorship concepts.
AI.motivation: The motivation for this paper is to address the increasingly prominent issues of authorship, credit attribution, and recognition of contributions to research software, particularly in fields where software is an essential part of the research process. The authors aim to provide a detailed and documented case study that can serve as a basis for discussing how existing guidelines are applied in practice and to identify potential tensions within the community.
AI.method: The method employed in this paper is a case study approach, which involves a detailed examination of a specific instance from lattice QCD research. The case study highlights the development of numerical strategies, long-term software infrastructure, and conceptual extensions, with a focus on the events, the role of software, and the interaction with established mechanisms for credit attribution and research integrity assessment.
AI.result: The result of the paper is a comprehensive analysis of the case study, which reveals the complex questions of authorship, priority, and credit attribution that arise when software plays a significant role in research. The paper does not discuss the underlying scientific results but instead emphasizes the practical aspects of collaboration and the challenges faced in recognizing contributions.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion drawn from the paper is that there is a need for further discussion and possibly the establishment of additional community standards to recognize long-term research software contributions. The paper serves as a call for more transparency and dialogue on the application of current practices and guidelines in the context of realistic collaborative environments, with an emphasis on the balance between open scientific collaboration, software sustainability, and traditional notions of authorship.

title: Exact chiral symmetry with quantum signal processing
summary: We give a quantum signal processing (QSP) algorithm for the overlap fermion Hamiltonian which preserves the Ginsparg-Wilson relation up to a controllable error $ε_e$. Quantum simulations of Dirac fermions with exact chiral symmetry are thus nearly free: applying the overlap Hamiltonian costs only a factor logarithmic in $ε_e$ more than the Wilson-Dirac Hamiltonian. Comparing to domain-wall fermions, a mild overhead is found in circuit complexity while reducing qubit costs. We show how QSP effectively constructs an extra dimension when simulating the overlap operator, illustrating that the scaling of quantum algorithms reflects the deeper physics of overlap fermions arising at the boundary of domain-wall fermions.

AI.tldr: A QSP algorithm for the overlap fermion Hamiltonian is presented, which maintains the Ginsparg-Wilson relation with a controllable error. This method allows for nearly cost-free quantum simulations of Dirac fermions with exact chiral symmetry, introducing a slight overhead in circuit complexity but reducing qubit costs when compared to domain-wall fermions. The QSP approach also demonstrates the creation of an extra dimension in the simulation, highlighting the physical relationship between overlap and domain-wall fermions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop a quantum signal processing (QSP) algorithm that can simulate the overlap fermion Hamiltonian while preserving the Ginsparg-Wilson relation within a controllable error margin, enabling efficient quantum simulations of Dirac fermions with exact chiral symmetry. The work aims to reduce the computational cost associated with such simulations, particularly in terms of qubit usage, as compared to the domain-wall fermions approach.
AI.method: The method involves the use of a QSP algorithm tailored for the overlap fermion Hamiltonian, ensuring that the Ginsparg-Wilson relation is preserved up to a small, controlled error. This approach minimizes the additional computational cost, with the application of the overlap Hamiltonian requiring only a logarithmic factor more resources than the Wilson-Dirac Hamiltonian. It also explores the construction of an extra dimension during the simulation, reflecting the underlying physics of overlap fermions.
AI.result: The result is a QSP-based quantum simulation method for the overlap fermion Hamiltonian that introduces a mild overhead in circuit complexity but significantly reduces the number of qubits required, as opposed to using domain-wall fermions. The algorithm effectively simulates an extra dimension, providing insight into the connection between overlap and domain-wall fermions from a physics perspective.
AI.conclusion: In conclusion, the QSP algorithm for the overlap fermion Hamiltonian offers a way to perform quantum simulations of Dirac fermions with exact chiral symmetry at a lower cost in terms of qubit usage. It does so with a minor increase in circuit complexity, and it also provides a deeper understanding of the physics behind overlap fermions, showing that they emerge at the boundary of domain-wall fermions.
